passage:
Dear Gargi Masi,
At Sunday lunch I told everyone about the night the roof leaked at Nani's house and we all slept in the kitchen by a lantern. I can see it: the drip into the steel bucket, your blue shawl over my feet, the smell of kerosene.
Then Mummy and you both said it never happened. Nani's house has a concrete roof, and I only stayed there in summer. I was hurt, honestly. It felt as if you were taking away something that was mine.
I've been thinking since. Maybe I built it from your stories about your own childhood there. It still feels so real that letting go of it is strange.
Could you tell me the lantern story again, properly? I want to know whose memory it is.
Love, Harsha

qa.q: What did Mummy and Gargi Masi say about the leaking roof?
qa.a: They said it never happened, since Nani's house has a concrete roof and Harsha only stayed there in summer.

qa.q: Why did Harsha feel hurt when told the leak never happened?
qa.a: The memory was so vivid, with the drip, the blue shawl and the kerosene smell, that losing it felt like having something taken away.

qa.q: What step does Harsha take towards understanding the memory?
qa.a: Harsha asks Gargi Masi to tell the lantern story again, properly, to find out whose memory it really is.

qa.q: How might Gargi Masi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She might be touched that her childhood stories stayed so strongly with Harsha, and a little sorry the correction at lunch hurt. 🤍

grounding: It shows a young adult with a vivid, emotional childhood memory that family members say never happened.

passage:
Rekha, is the mic on? Okay. My strangest memory: I was sure I got lost at the zoo when I was four. I can see the tall bars, a zookeeper in a green cap, and an announcement with my name, Simran, echoing everywhere.
I told that story at every sleepover. Last year at a family wedding I told it again, and my dad said, "Simran, we never took you to the zoo at four. You got lost in a shop for two minutes." My brother nodded. Two minutes!
I actually argued with them. The green cap felt more real than my own birthday.
It shook me. If something that vivid can come from my own head, what else can? I still love the story. I just call it "my zoo story" now, not "the day I got lost".

qa.q: Where did Simran's dad say Simran really got lost?
qa.a: In a shop, for two minutes.

qa.q: Why did Simran argue with the family at first?
qa.a: The green cap and the echoing announcement felt more real than Simran's own birthday, so the memory seemed impossible to doubt.

qa.q: How does Simran choose to hold the memory now?
qa.a: Simran still enjoys it but calls it "my zoo story" instead of "the day I got lost", treating it as a story rather than proof.

qa.q: How might Simran's dad have felt correcting the story at the wedding?
qa.a: He may have felt amused or a bit awkward correcting a favourite story in front of relatives, while wanting the facts straight.

grounding: It shows a young adult whose detailed, emotional childhood memory is said by family never to have happened.

passage:
I'm Kiran, Salma's roommate, so I heard this one live. Salma was video-calling her family and said, "Remember when Abbu carried me on his shoulders through the flood water? I was holding the umbrella." She described it all: the brown water, the red umbrella, the shop shutters.
Her mother went quiet. Then her brother said, "Salma, there was never a flood. You saw that in a film at Khala's house."
Salma laughed at first, then didn't. After the call she sat on her bed for a long time with her knees pulled up. She said, "I can still feel the umbrella handle."
I don't know what was going on in her head. I just made tea and didn't take either side.

qa.q: What colour was the umbrella in Salma's memory?
qa.a: The umbrella was red.

qa.q: What might Salma be feeling as she sits with her knees pulled up?
qa.a: She seems unsettled and confused, because the memory feels real enough to touch, yet her family says it never happened.

qa.q: What could help Salma make sense of the memory?
qa.a: She could ask her family calmly about the film at Khala's house, and treat the memory as meaningful without needing every detail to be true.

qa.q: How does Kiran respond, and why might that help Salma?
qa.a: Kiran makes tea and takes neither side, which gives Salma space to feel unsettled without being pushed.

grounding: It shows a roommate watching a young adult describe a vivid childhood scene that her family says never occurred.

passage:
Saturday: At Diwali lunch at Nani's house in Jodhpur, Irawati, twenty, told the table about the peacock. "I was four. It walked right into this courtyard, spread its tail, and I fed it a bit of my roti. I can still hear it screaming." Nani laughed. "No peacock ever came here, beti. Never." Irawati's mother shook her head too.
Monday: Back at college, Irawati couldn't let it go. She told her friend Asif, "I can see the blue of its neck. How can that not be real?" Asif shrugged. "Maybe you saw one somewhere else?"
Thursday: Her mother phoned. She had found an old album: Irawati, four, at a zoo in Delhi, holding roti out to a peacock behind a fence. Irawati looked at the photo for a long time. The feeling was real. The courtyard wasn't.

qa.q: What did Irawati say she fed the peacock?
qa.a: A bit of her roti.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Nani said no peacock came, and why?
qa.a: Irawati felt puzzled and unsettled, unable to let it go, because she could still see the blue of its neck and hear it scream.

qa.q: What did the old photo show, and how could Irawati use that lesson?
qa.a: It showed her feeding a peacock at a zoo in Delhi; she could remember that vivid details can be real pieces placed in the wrong scene, and check before insisting.

qa.q: What might Nani have felt when Irawati insisted about the courtyard?
qa.a: Nani was probably amused but certain, knowing her own courtyard well, and perhaps curious where the story came from 🙂

grounding: A young woman vividly recalls a childhood scene her family says never happened there, learning that vividness does not prove accuracy.

passage: Simran, beti, you told that well story again at dinner, eyes shining: you, six years old, falling into the farm well, the cold water, your Dadu pulling you out by your plait. You told it so well your cousins went quiet. Now let your Rekha Dadi tell you what I remember, since I was there. There was no fall. It was your cousin Gunjan who slipped into the irrigation channel, knee-deep, and your Dadu lifted her out, laughing. You were on the charpai with me, eating a guava, and you cried because everyone ran to Gunjan. For years afterwards you begged to hear that story. Somewhere along the way it became yours. I'm not saying you're lying, beti. Your heart remembers the fright. But a memory can be bright and strong and still not have happened.

qa.q: Who actually slipped into the irrigation channel?
qa.a: Her cousin Gunjan, knee-deep.

qa.q: Why does Simran's well story feel so real to her?
qa.a: She heard the family story so often and felt the fright of that day so strongly that the vivid version became her own memory.

qa.q: How could Simran hold this memory differently from now on?
qa.a: She could treat the feeling as real but the details as uncertain, and check with family before telling it as fact.

qa.q: What might it be like for Gunjan to hear Simran tell the story as her own?
qa.a: Gunjan might be puzzled or a little put out, hearing her own scary moment told as someone else's.

grounding: A grandmother tells a young woman that her vivid, emotional childhood memory of falling into a well never happened to her.
